options: An abstraction layer inside sqlservr.exe handling scheduling, memory management, and I/O completion
A separate Windows service that replaces the OS kernel
A GUI tool for configuring SQL Server
A synonym for SQL Server Agent
questions.explain: SQLOS is not a separate process — it's a layer of code inside the Database Engine process that the rest of the Engine calls into instead of calling OS APIs directly.

questions.q: How does SQLOS scheduling differ from ordinary preemptive OS scheduling?
options: It's non-preemptive: a worker runs until it voluntarily yields, rather than being forcibly interrupted
It's identical to Windows thread scheduling with no differences
It assigns every task to a single shared scheduler regardless of core count
It only runs one query at a time across the whole instance
questions.explain: SQLOS schedulers are cooperative — a worker keeps running until it hits a natural yield point like a lock wait or a page read.

questions.q: How many SQLOS schedulers does an instance typically create?
options: One per logical CPU core visible to the instance
Exactly one, regardless of core count
One per database on the instance
One per user connection
questions.explain: Each logical CPU core gets its own scheduler, and each scheduler manages its own pool of workers and runnable queue.

questions.q: What does the SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD wait type indicate?
options: A task voluntarily gave up its scheduler turn to let other queued tasks run
A query encountered a syntax error
A disk read failed
A login authentication was rejected
questions.explain: High volumes of SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD typically point to CPU pressure — tasks running long enough between voluntary yields that others queue up behind them.

questions.q: Besides scheduling, what other two responsibilities does SQLOS own?
options: Memory management and asynchronous I/O completion
Backup compression and encryption key management
User authentication and permission checks
T-SQL parsing and query plan caching
questions.explain: SQLOS requests memory from the OS and distributes it to internal consumers like the buffer pool, and it issues asynchronous I/O so workers aren't blocked waiting on disk.
